record.paper_title: Twenty open problems in quantum control
record.context_brief: Continuous measurement-based feedback versus direct coherent feedback
record.original_question: For a quantum system controlled either by continuous measurement-based feedback or by coherent feedback implemented through direct system-auxiliary coupling, what is the exact relationship between the two control paradigms when both are given the same dissipative resources? Is coherent feedback through direct coupling superior to continuous measurement-based feedback under those conditions, and if it is superior, does the advantage remain when the added dissipative resources are removed?

evidence.quote: Feedback control via continuous measurements is an example of an irreversible Markovian coupling between the primary system and the auxiliary. The efficacy of field-mediated control can therefore be compared directly with that of feedback control via continuous measurements. But a comparison between the latter and coherent feedback control implemented solely with direct (unitary) coupling between the two is only meaningful if unitary and irreversible couplings can be compared.

Problem 2: What is the precise relationship between continuous measurement-based feedback, and coherent feedback via direct system-auxiliary coupling given the same dissipative resources? Is the latter superior to the former, and if so, does this remain true without the dissipative resources?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a quantum system S (the "primary" system) coupled to an auxiliary quantum system A, with the goal of stabilizing, preparing, or otherwise controlling the state of S. Two distinct feedback paradigms are available:

(i) Continuous measurement-based feedback: A is continuously measured (a Markovian, irreversible coupling that produces a classical measurement record), and the measurement record is used in real time to modulate Hamiltonian or other parameters acting on S. Mathematically the joint evolution is described by a stochastic master equation conditioned on the measurement record, with an actuation Hamiltonian H_c(t) that is a (causal) functional of the record.

(ii) Coherent feedback via direct system–auxiliary coupling: S and A are coupled only through a unitary (Hamiltonian) interaction H_SA, with no measurement performed. The reduced dynamics of S are obtained by tracing over A, and any irreversible (dissipative) channels acting on A or S are specified explicitly as part of the model.

Assume that in both paradigms the same dissipative resources are available: i.e., the same Lindblad dissipators acting on S and A (with the same rates) are present, so that the only structural difference between the two setups is whether the S–A coupling is mediated by measurement-plus-classical-control or by a direct Hamiltonian interaction.

Questions:
(a) Determine the precise mathematical relationship between paradigms (i) and (ii) under this matched-resource assumption. Specifically, characterize the set of completely positive trace-preserving evolutions of S that can be realized by (i) and the set realizable by (ii), and determine whether one set is contained in the other.

(b) Decide whether paradigm (ii) is strictly superior to paradigm (i) for some control task (for example, achieving strictly higher steady-state fidelity to a target state, or strictly faster convergence) when both have access to the same dissipative resources.

(c) If (ii) is strictly superior in part (b), determine whether this superiority persists when the shared dissipative resources are removed, i.e., when in (ii) only the unitary S–A coupling (and the intrinsic dissipation of S) is retained while in (i) only the measurement of A and the corresponding classical actuation on S is retained.
artifact.status_search_result: Substantial progress has been made on comparing coherent and measurement-based feedback. For linear quantum systems, work by Yamamoto (2014) shows coherent feedback can exactly match measurement-based feedback performance with ideal controllers and can also achieve tasks measurement-based feedback cannot. Experimental and theoretical comparisons (e.g., Liu et al., Phys. Rev. X 6, 011022 (2016)) study driven-dissipative vs. measurement-based entanglement stabilization, and other works (e.g., Phys. Rev. A 97, 062341) replace measurement feedback by coherent feedback for state preparation. However, a fully general resource-matched characterization for arbitrary nonlinear quantum systems—including the question of whether coherent feedback's advantage persists once shared dissipative resources are removed—does not appear to be settled in full generality, so the problem as posed is partially solved.

status_evidence.title: Coherent versus measurement feedback: Linear systems theory for quantum information
status_evidence.snippet: Coherent feedback can exactly match measurement-based feedback performance under a fair comparison with ideal controllers, and achieves tasks impossible for measurement-based feedback.
status_evidence.claim: For linear quantum systems the relationship has been characterized: coherent feedback is at least as powerful, strictly more so for some tasks.

status_evidence.title: Comparing and Combining Measurement-Based and Driven-Dissipative Entanglement Stabilization
status_evidence.snippet: Comparison of measurement-based and driven-dissipative (coherent) approaches to entanglement stabilization, finding higher fidelity for driven-dissipative due to lower latency.
status_evidence.claim: For specific tasks, coherent/driven-dissipative feedback empirically outperforms measurement-based feedback when given comparable resources.

status_evidence.title: Coherent vs. measurement-based feedback for controlling a single qubit
status_evidence.snippet: Direct comparison for single-qubit control of the two feedback paradigms.
status_evidence.claim: Targeted comparisons exist for specific small systems, but no general resource-matched theorem has been established.

status_evidence.title: Replacing measurement feedback with coherent feedback for quantum state preparation
status_evidence.snippet: Shows coherent feedback can replace measurement feedback for state-preparation tasks.
status_evidence.claim: Partial equivalence/replacement results are known for specific tasks.
